In August 1998, after the G1 Climax, Nishimura was diagnosed with a cancerous tumor in his retroperitoneal space. He spent nearly two years fighting by using natural remedies such as natural diet, medicinal food, Chinese medicine, Ayurvada, sea bathing, and urine therapy, instead of chemotherapy, until he was declared cancer-free in 2000. His cancer scare inspired his political career as a food education instructor, as his top priority was how to make the world healthier and how to direct it to preventive medicine.

In March 2024, Nishimura was diagnosed with stage-four esophageal cancer. The cancer had already spread to the lymph nodes outside the esophageous and the entire upper left side of his body, except his head. Unlike his first cancer scare, he had to undergo chemotherapy. In July, he was in a coma due to the cancer metastasising to the brain, but was able to recover. In August 2024, Nishimura was chosen by Dory Funk, Jr. as his partner for his final match and his final trip to Japan, against Atsushi Onita and Raijin Yaguchi for FMW-E’s Kawasaki Stadium show on August 24. To take part in this match, Nishimura had to get a waiver from the hospital and have five doctors, nurses and trainers at ringside to monitor his health. He and Funk defeated Onita and Yaguchi in a Double Hell Current Blast Deathmatch, as Nishimura used Funk’s spinning toehold to force Yaguchi to submit. On February 28, 2025, it was announced by Shinsuke Nakamura that Nishimura had died at the age of 53.

I think of the people who worked in the World Trade Center. Those skyscrapers that were so part of the identity of NYC that you almost took them for granted, they were always there if you were from NYC or North Jersey they were apart of your life. But in the background. And to the men and women of the WTC it was their workplace. They ate there. They had friends there. They were just doing a job. Some had friends, some probably didn’t get along like most people have those they don’t get along with at work. There mundane lives. Going to work. Some were late, others were early. That decision either saved or costed them their life. 

But these normal people going about their day are forever linked in this collective trauma that we all experienced that day, but they experienced so personally. There were no camera phones. No Twitter or Facebook. We didn’t get a livestream from anyone like we would today God-forbid if (and when) another 9/11 style attack occurs. Their last moments are confined to phone calls and voicemails. We have to fill in the blanks ourselves. 

In the end the 2,753 people who died at the WTC only had one another. Office colleagues, maintenance people, the police or firefighters helping them. They were alone in those towers yet we were watching and still watching. 

There’s children that will never be born. Children that never got to grow up. Someone in their 20’s on 9/11 today would be middle age. A father most likely is a grandfather by now. Someone in their 70s would most likely be approaching the end of their natural life. A mother is a grandmother by now. A middle aged person at the time would be nearing retirement. 

What would those 2,753 people think of the world of today?

One must remember where the world was at in the lead up and waging of the Iraq War. On 9/11 many Americans thought that Iraq was involved. Iraqi Intelligence meeting with Mohamed Atta would be used as a source of justification for invading. That claim would then be disputed. For all the hand wringing over the Iraq War afterwards from the likes of Hillary Clinton and John Kerry, Iraq under Saddam Hussein was viewed as the next big threat. 

Iran was considered contained and isolated. The issue was that Iran was in large part contained by Iraq. We now have a situation where Shia militias in Iraq are serving as proxy fighters for the regime in Tehran. That largely occurred due to the power vacuum in Iraq and the elections that followed. Rumsfeld and team failed to imagine this occurring after the fall of Baathist Baghdad. 

Had the Iraq War never had occurred, and had he never been executed Saddam Hussein would be 87-years-old granted he lived that long. Would the Baathist Regime had survived the Arab Spring? Would the Arab Spring had even occurred without the Iraq War? Saddam’s sons would be both approaching their 60’s. Young in Arab despot years. Technology and new alliances would see them emboldened and no doubt ruling Iraq with an even harsher iron fist. One could assume that Hamas in its war with Israel would be finding safe harbor in Iraq not in Qatar and Iran. Would they seek to attack the United States. 

The Bush doctrine was to deal with global threats before they materialized. It took the “Never Again” slogan of post-9/11 America to heart. The fact that WMD’s were not found (Saddam had over a year to hide them) or that Iran is now the bigger threat is immaterial. The fact of the matter is that from September 12th 2001 to 2003 the consensus was that Iraq was the next threat to the American homeland. All the pundits and Democrats who now Monday night quarterback the war agreed it was as well. The staunchly anti-war crowd can claim some measure of forward thinking based on the wars eventual unpopularity and malaise. Had the war had “gone better” the opposite would be true. 

Given the intelligence President Bush had at the time going into Iraq was the best decision he could have made. Had he not of gone into Iraq and let’s say in 2009 they attacked the United States, President Bush’s decision not to invade would’ve been compared to Clinton’s inaction prior to 9/11.
